subject: How to convert estimated precision to variance?

messages.author: fd5c6f6a19cd1661
messages.subject: How to convert estimated precision to variance?
parts:
Dear INLA-community,

I have a simple model in INLA (the regressor is a single model=iid term), which reports the precision of the hyperparameter. How to convert it to variance?

Question #1: Is my understanding correct that the CI can be simply converted by taking the reciprocal of the endpoints? (As reciprocal is an invertible monotone transformation: https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/187154/does-invertible-monotone-transformation-of-a-confidence-interval-give-you-a-conf )

Question #2: What to do with the point estimator? This is not an MLE, thus no invariance principle applies, so, if my understanding is correct, I can't simple take its reciprocal.

Thank you in advance,
Tamas

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to convert estimated precision to variance?
parts:
If you're into quantiles, you can always convert those directly. if
you're into the mode or mean, that is something else.

INLA report the values of the precisions. Internally it reports the
values for the log(precision), and its easier (AND more stable and
accurate) to start from there. There are functions for all this, as
shown in the small example below.



> r = inla(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y = 1:10))
> summary(r)

Call:
"inla(formula = y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y = 1:10))"

Time used:
Pre-processing Running inla Post-processing Total
0.4276 0.1422 0.0257 0.5955

Fixed effects:
mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld
(Intercept) 5.5 0.9583 3.5866 5.5 7.4103 5.5 0

The model has no random effects

Model hyperparameters:
mean sd 0.025quant
0.5quant
Precision for the Gaussian observations 0.1327
0.0553 0.0465 0.1252
0.975quant mode
Precision for the Gaussian observations 0.2609 0.1092

Expected number of effective parameters(std dev): 1.00(0.00)
Number of equivalent replicates : 10.00

Marginal log-Likelihood: -35.84
> m = r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]
> m.var = inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/exp(x), m)
> inla.zmarginal(m.var)
Mean 9.12902
Stdev 4.6752
Quantile 0.025 3.76885
Quantile 0.25 6.00863
Quantile 0.5 7.96542
Quantile 0.75 10.8579
Quantile 0.975 21.4395
> plot(inla.smarginal(m.var), type="l")

## the mode
> inla.mmarginal(m.var)
[1] 6.355539937

## quantiles
> q = seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)
> inla.qmarginal(q, m.var)
[1] 4.765569102 5.624929102 6.383794106 7.143767740 7.965420916
[6] 8.916443633 10.107438123 11.781429701 14.749054594

## which you can also get directly

> rev(1/exp(inla.qmarginal(q, m)))
[1] 4.779765995 5.641906096 6.402697047 7.164466222 7.988069169
[6] 8.941487020 10.135856027 11.815668573 14.798734751


as you see, there is a little loss of accuracy, due to the internal
finite representation of the marginal, but the one using 'm' is the
most correct one.


H
